Reptiles
Which features are shared by all members of the Class Reptilia?
Ectothermic, breathe air, internal fertilisation
Endothermic, breathe air, internal fertilisation
Ectothermic, breathe through gills, external fertilisation
Endothermic, breathe air, external fertilisation
All reptiles are ectothermic, have a backbone, breathe air and have internal fertilisation of the egg.
Crocodiles
What are the bony scales on a crocodile's back called?
Osteoderms
Scutes
Odontoids
Chromatophores
The back of the crocodile is covered in protective scales called osteoderms (meaning bony skin).
Crocodiles
Which member of the order Crocodylia is found in southern Africa?
Only the Nile crocodile
The Nile crocodile and the caiman
The Nile crocodile and the alligator
The Nile crocodile and the gavial
Crocodylia includes crocodiles, caimans, alligators and gavials, but the Nile crocodile is the only species found in southern Africa.
Crocodiles
How many chambers does a crocodile's heart have?
Four
Three
Two
Five
Unlike other reptiles but similar to mammals and birds, crocodiles have a four-chambered heart.
Crocodiles
Roughly what part of a crocodile's total length is made up by the tail?
Crocodiles can exceed 6 m in length, and 40% of this is the tail.
Crocodiles
Why must a crocodile lift its head to open its mouth when basking?
The upper jaw is fused with the skull
The lower jaw is fused with the skull
Its jaw-opening muscles are too strong
Its teeth lock the jaws together
Because the upper jaw is fused with the skull, the head must be lifted to let the bottom jaw fall open (mouth-gaping).
Crocodiles
Why do crocodiles lie on the bank with their mouths open?
To warm or cool the blood through the mouth membranes
To let their teeth dry out in the sun
To show other crocodiles their territory
To catch insects that fly past
The thick hide slows heat transfer, so the soft mouth membrane absorbs heat; the same mechanism, facing away from the sun, cools the crocodile.
Crocodiles
In which river in south-eastern Botswana do Nile crocodiles occur?
Limpopo
Boteti
Okavango
Chobe
Crocodiles occur in northern Botswana (Okavango, Chobe, Zambezi, Kubango) and, in the south east, in the Limpopo.
Crocodiles
About how much of the food a crocodile eats is stored as fat?
About 60%
About 10%
About 30%
About 90%
About 60% of the food they eat is stored as fat in the tail, organs, abdomen and along the back.
Crocodiles
How long can a newly hatched crocodile survive on the yolk reserves in its belly?
Up to four months
Up to one week
Up to two years
Up to one month
A newly hatched crocodile can survive for up to four months on the fat reserves of the egg-yolk in its belly.
Crocodiles
What does the gular flap at the back of the throat allow a crocodile to do?
Open its mouth under water
Swallow prey under water
Breathe under water
Chew its food
The gular flap closes when submerging, allowing the crocodile to open its mouth under water, but it must surface before swallowing.
Crocodiles
How does the bite force of a crocodile compare with that of a hyaena?
More than six times stronger
About half as strong
About the same
Slightly weaker
A hyaena bites at around 800 pounds per square inch, while a crocodile bites at over 5000, more than six times more powerful.
Crocodiles
What is the first chamber of a crocodile's stomach called, where swallowed stones help grind food?
The gizzard
The crop
The rumen
The gular
Ingested stones end up in the first of the two stomach chambers, the gizzard, where muscles and stones grind up the food.
Crocodiles
What do sub-adult crocodiles (3 to 12 years old) mainly eat?
Fish
Insects and spiders
Large mammals
Plants
Sub-adults of 3-12 years eat mainly fish, but also small vertebrates such as young crocodiles, lizards, birds and small mammals.
Crocodiles
What is unusual about the strength of a crocodile's jaw muscles?
Very strong when closing but weak when opening
Very strong when opening but weak when closing
Equally weak when opening and closing
Only strong when the crocodile is under water
The jaw muscles of the crocodile are extremely strong when closing but lack strength when opening.
Crocodiles
How far from the water's edge can a crocodile lunge out of the water?
Up to 3 m
Up to 30 cm
Up to 10 m
Up to 20 m
Crocodiles can propel themselves out of the water at 70 km/h in a lunge up to 3 m from the water's edge.
Crocodiles
At about what age do Nile crocodiles reach sexual maturity?
About 12 years
About 2 years
About 5 years
About 25 years
Males and females reach sexual maturity at approximately 12 years (males about 3 m, females just over 2 m).
Crocodiles
Why does a female crocodile urinate on her nest during incubation?
To prevent the eggs from drying out
To mark her territory for the male
To warm the eggs
To keep the hatchlings' sex female
During incubation she urinates on the nest to prevent egg dehydration.
Crocodiles
According to the manual, what sex will a crocodile embryo be if the nest is 26-30 °C?
Female
Male
Half male, half female
The temperature has no effect
With temperature-dependent sex determination, 26-30 °C produces females and 31-34 °C produces males.
Crocodiles
Roughly what percentage of crocodiles that hatch survive to adulthood?
About 1%
About 10%
About 25%
About 50%
Roughly 1% of crocodiles that hatch survive until adulthood.
Crocodiles
In Botswana, which crocodiles may be destroyed legally?
Only known man-eaters
Any crocodile over 4 m long
Crocodiles outside the Okavango Delta
Any crocodile during the dry season
In Botswana crocodiles are protected and only known man-eaters are destroyed legally.
Snakes
How can snakes be told apart from legless lizards?
Snakes have no eyelids and no external ears
Snakes have eyelids and external ears
Snakes have no scales on the belly
Snakes have two equal-sized lungs
Serpentes can be distinguished from legless lizards by their lack of eyelids and external ears.
Snakes
Where does a snake place the fork of its tongue to interpret scents?
Into the organ of Jacobson in the roof of the mouth
Into the nostrils on the snout
Into the heat pits on the lips
Into the venom glands behind the eyes
The tongue picks up scent particles and the fork is inserted into the organ of Jacobson, a smelling organ in the roof of the mouth.
Snakes
What helps a snake to detect ground-borne vibrations?
Its large body contact with the ground and hollow ribs and backbone
Its large external ears
Its keen eyesight and movable eyelids
The organ of Jacobson in its mouth
The large body surface touching the ground, with the hollow rib bones and backbone, conducts vibrations that nerve endings detect.
Snake venom
What is snake venom, according to the manual?
Modified saliva
Modified blood
Stomach acid
Modified sweat
Venom is modified saliva stored in glands that run from behind the eyes to the back of the head.
Snake venom
Which snakes does the manual give as examples of cytotoxic venom?
Spitting cobras and most adders
Mambas and most cobras
Vine snake and boomslang
Pythons and mole snakes
Cytotoxic venom is found in spitting cobras and most adders, including the puff adder.
Snake venom
How does cytotoxic venom act?
It breaks down cell tissue, causing necrosis
It shuts down the nervous system
It stops the blood from clotting
It paralyses only the eyes
Cytotoxins cause necrosis by breaking down cell tissue around the bite, and can continue to kill blood and other cells, often causing organ failure.
Snake venom
Neurotoxic venom mainly shuts down which muscles?
The involuntary muscles
The jaw muscles only
The leg muscles only
The muscles around the bite only
Neurotoxins attack the nervous system, shutting down primarily the involuntary muscles in the body.
Snake venom
Which of these is a symptom of neurotoxic venom listed in the manual?
Difficulty in speech and breathing
Bleeding from the body orifices
Rotting of the tissue around the bite
Blood clots forming at the bite
Neurotoxic symptoms include vomiting, abnormal sweating, blurred vision, difficulty in speech and breathing and loss of consciousness.
Snake venom
How does haemotoxic venom act at first?
As an anti-coagulant that stops blood clotting
As a nerve poison that stops breathing
As a pain-killer that numbs the bite
As a muscle poison that causes cramps
Haemotoxins (vine snake and boomslang) act initially as an anti-coagulant, causing serious internal bleeding and haemorrhaging.
Snake venom
Apart from internal bleeding, what else can cause death from a boomslang bite?
Blood clots in the brain
Failure of the involuntary muscles
Blindness from venom in the eyes
Loss of a limb from necrosis
Boomslang venom also has a pro-coagulant element, so death may result from internal haemorrhaging or blood clotting in the brain.
Snake safety
How should you roll a log when collecting firewood?
So the log stays between you and what is under it
Towards yourself so you can see underneath
With your bare hands from the far side
By kicking it over quickly
The log should be rolled so that it remains between the person and whatever lies below it.
Snake safety
Why should you not touch a snake that appears to be dead?
Some reptiles pretend to be dead (thanatosis)
Dead snakes carry dangerous diseases
Venom becomes stronger after death
It is illegal to touch dead snakes
Some reptiles use thanatosis (pretending to be dead) as a means of defence.
Snake safety
Why are puff adders particularly dangerous to people walking in the bush?
They lie on pathways and do not move off readily
They chase people over long distances
They spit venom into the eyes
They drop from trees onto people
Puff adders are often found lying in the sun on pathways and do not move off readily when approached.
Snake safety
Why are black mambas considered among the most dangerous snakes?
Fast, long striking range, nervous, fastest-acting venom
Slow, lie on paths and do not move off
They spit venom into the eyes from far away
Their fangs stab sideways when they are held
Black mambas are extremely fast, have a long striking range, a nervous disposition and the fastest-acting venom of our snakes.
Snake safety
What is the most effective first aid when a spitting cobra spits venom into someone's eyes?
Flush the eyes with water or another bland liquid, then get medical help
Rub the eyes firmly and wait for the pain to pass
Cover the eyes with a tight bandage and rest
Inject antivenom directly into the eyes
The most effective treatment is to flush the eyes with water or any other bland liquid and then seek medical help.
Snake safety
Why is identifying the snake not critical after a snakebite?
Bites are generally treated according to the symptoms
All snakes have the same venom
All snakebites are harmless
Antivenom works for every species
Bites are generally treated symptomatically, so identification is helpful but not critical; do not put yourself in danger trying.
Snake movement
Which type of snake movement is used by heavy-bodied snakes such as puff adders and mature pythons?
Rectilinear (caterpillar-like) motion
Side winding
Concertina motion
Arboreal gliding
Rectilinear motion, in a straight line using the belly scales, is used by heavy-bodied species such as puff adders and mature pythons.
Snake movement
Which is the most common type of snake movement, being the fastest and most energy efficient?
Serpentine motion (lateral undulation)
Rectilinear motion
Concertina motion
Side winding
Most snakes use serpentine motion, gliding in an S shape, as it is the fastest and most energy-efficient method.
Snake movement
Concertina motion is mainly used by which kind of snake?
Burrowing snakes, such as the burrowing asp
Tree snakes, such as the boomslang
Desert dune snakes
Heavy snakes such as pythons
Concertina motion is a specialised locomotion restricted to burrowing snakes such as the burrowing asp.
Snake movement
In southern Africa, side winding is restricted to which snake?
Peringuey's desert adder
Puff adder
Black mamba
Southern African python
Side winding is a specialised locomotion that, in southern Africa, is restricted to Peringuey's desert adder on loose dune sand.
Snake feeding
Why do snakes usually swallow their prey head first?
So fur, feathers or skin flow the right way
So the prey cannot see the snake
So the venom reaches the brain first
So the snake can chew the head
Prey is usually swallowed head first so that fur, feathers or outer skin flow in the correct direction for easy swallowing.
Snake feeding
How does a snake avoid suffocating while swallowing large prey?
It extends its windpipe beyond the jaw
It holds its breath for several days
It breathes through its skin
It breathes through its tail
The trachea (windpipe) can be extended out beyond the jaw to prevent suffocation while swallowing large prey.
Snake feeding
Most snakes can swallow prey up to what proportion of their own body weight?
Most snakes can swallow prey up to 25% of their body weight; pythons can eat their own weight.
Snake feeding
What is special about the digestion of pythons compared with other snakes?
They also digest horn, hair and feathers
They cannot digest bones
They regurgitate all the fur and feathers
They digest food only with venom
Most snakes regurgitate hair, feathers and horn, but pythons are the exception and digest even these.
Snake safety
Why should a snake not be held by the tail during capture?
It can damage the snake's vertebrae
The tail contains venom glands
The tail breaks off easily like a lizard's
The snake will die of shock
If possible a snake should not be held by the tail as this can damage its vertebrae; a grab stick should be used.
Highly venomous snakes
What does the manual say about the Cape cobra's venom?
It is the most potent neurotoxin in southern Africa
It is a cytotoxin that it can spit over 2 m
It is a haemotoxin with no antivenom
It is mild and not dangerous to people
The Cape cobra cannot spit, but its venom is the most potent neurotoxin in southern Africa, second only to the boomslang in potency.
Highly venomous snakes
How are Anchieta's cobra and the snouted cobra best told apart?
By their separate distributions
By the colour of their bellies
By the shape of their hoods
By their venom type
The two look very similar and are best separated on their mutually independent distributions.
Highly venomous snakes
What type of venom does the Mozambique spitting cobra have?
Cytotoxic
Neurotoxic
Haemotoxic
It is non-venomous
The Mozambique spitting cobra is oviparous and has a deadly cytotoxic venom.
Highly venomous snakes
Which features help identify a black mamba?
Black lining inside the mouth and a coffin-shaped head
Bright green body and very large eyes
Black and red band through the eye
Orange body with dark bands
The black mamba has a black lining to the inside of the mouth and a coffin-shaped head; its body is grey to brown.
Highly venomous snakes
What type of venom does the shield-nosed snake have?
Neurotoxic
Haemotoxic
Cytotoxic
It is non-venomous
The shield-nosed snake is a short cobra with neurotoxic venom; bites are rare but neurological symptoms are reported.
Highly venomous snakes
In Botswana, how do male and female boomslangs differ in colour?
Males are bright green; females are duller brown
Females are bright green; males are duller brown
Both sexes are grey with black blotches
Both sexes are black with white bands
Boomslang are dimorphic; in Botswana the female is a duller brownish colour and the male is a striking green.
Highly venomous snakes
What allows the boomslang to see stationary prey?
Its very large eyes and exceptional eyesight
Heat pits on its lips
Its long forked tongue
Vibrations through its hollow ribs
The boomslang's eyes are noticeably larger than other snakes', and its exceptional eyesight lets it see stationary prey.
Highly venomous snakes
Which highly venomous snake has a bold black and red eye-band and no available antivenom?
Vine snake
Boomslang
Cape cobra
Puff adder
The vine (twig) snake is grey with black blotching and a black and red eye-band; its haemotoxic venom has no available antivenom.
Highly venomous snakes
Why should you never try to grab a stiletto snake behind the head?
It can stab your fingers with its fangs by flexing its neck
It will spit venom into your eyes
Its skin produces a poison
It will shed its tail and escape
Stiletto snakes can stab the fingers of anyone holding them behind the head with just a flex of the neck.
Highly venomous snakes
What does the manual say about the venom of the southern stiletto snake?
Cytotoxic and non-lethal, but can lead to amputations
Neurotoxic and the fastest acting in Africa
Haemotoxic with no antivenom
It has no venom at all
The stiletto snake's venom is cytotoxic but non-lethal; however, amputations after handling mishaps are not uncommon.
Highly venomous snakes
How does the puff adder reproduce?
It is viviparous, giving birth to live young
It lays eggs in termite mounds
It lays eggs and guards them
It lays eggs in water
Puff adders are viviparous and the live young are born 15-20 cm long.
Highly venomous snakes
Which snake is the most widely distributed in southern Africa?
Puff adder
Black mamba
Cape cobra
Vine snake
The puff adder is the most widely distributed snake in southern Africa, found in every habitat from almost true desert to forest.
Mildly and non-venomous snakes
How does a python's constriction kill its prey?
By causing heart failure and suffocation
By breaking all the prey's bones
By injecting venom while coiling
By drowning it in water
Contrary to popular belief, constriction does not break bones but rather causes heart failure and suffocation.
Mildly and non-venomous snakes
What does a female python do while her eggs incubate?
Coils around the eggs and does not eat
Leaves the eggs buried and unguarded
Carries the eggs in her mouth
Hunts more often to build up fat
She coils around the eggs, leaving only to bask or drink, and does not eat during the roughly 3-month incubation.
Mildly and non-venomous snakes
Which snake is orange with dark bands and has large eyes with vertical pupils?
Common tiger snake
Spotted bush snake
Mole snake
Angolan green snake
The common tiger snake is orange with dark bands and has large eyes with vertical pupils; it is non-venomous but bites readily.
Mildly and non-venomous snakes
How does the mole snake reproduce?
It gives birth to 25-50 live young
It lays up to 100 eggs in a termite mound
It lays two hard-shelled eggs
It lays eggs that the male guards
Mole snakes are viviparous, giving birth to 25-50 live young, and in exceptional cases 90 or more.
Mildly and non-venomous snakes
Which snake has black barring on the front two-thirds of its body and is mildly venomous?
Spotted bush snake
Angolan green snake
Boomslang
Common tiger snake
The spotted bush snake is green to olive-green with black barring on the front two-thirds of the body and is mildly venomous.
Mildly and non-venomous snakes
Where in Botswana does the Angolan green snake live?
The Delta and riverine areas of the north
The Central Kalahari
The south-western dunes
Rocky hills in the south east
The Angolan green snake lives in the Delta and riverine areas of northern Botswana, foraging along water courses.
Lizards
What is autotomy in lizards?
Shedding the tail when in danger
Changing skin colour
Pretending to be dead
Laying eggs without mating
Many lizards can shed their tails when in danger; this is called autotomy.
Lizards
Which skink does the manual give as an example of a viviparous (live-bearing) skink?
Kalahari burrowing skink
Kalahari tree skink
Snake-eyed skink
Rock skink
Skinks may be viviparous (Kalahari burrowing skinks) or oviparous (Kalahari tree skinks).
Lizards
How do monitor lizards use their tails in defence?
They lash with them; the tail cannot be shed
They shed them to distract predators
They wave them to look like a head
They use them to spray a foul liquid
Monitor lizards cannot shed their tails, but the tails can inflict serious injury on would-be predators.
Lizards
Where do Nile monitors frequently lay their eggs?
In termite mounds
In rock cracks
In tree cavities
In floating nests on water
Nile monitors dig into termite mounds to lay their eggs; the termites seal the hole, protecting the eggs and keeping them warm and humid.
Lizards
How does the white-throated monitor's habitat differ from the Nile monitor's?
It spends more time in trees and is seldom near water
It spends more time in water than on land
It lives only underground in burrows
It lives only on sandbanks in rivers
White-throated (rock or tree) monitors spend more time in trees than Nile monitors and are very seldom found near water.
Lizards
What is the principal diet of agamas?
Ants
Fish
Fruit
Rodents
Agamas are diurnal lizards whose principal diet is ants; males are brightly coloured and territorial.
Lizards
Which lizards live on rocky outcrops, have spiny scales and give birth to live young?
Girdled lizards
Old world lizards
Skinks
Geckos
Girdled lizards have strong spiny scales, live on rocky outcrops, hide in narrow crevices and are viviparous.
Lizards
How do geckos clean their eyes?
With their tongues
By blinking their eyelids
With their front feet
By rubbing them on rocks
Geckos have fixed eyelids and clean their eyes with their tongues.
Lizards
Apart from geckos, which is the only other reptile that can vocalise?
The crocodile
The chameleon
The leopard tortoise
The python
All geckos are vocal; apart from geckos, the crocodile is the only other reptile that can vocalise.
Lizards
Where does a chameleon hold its hollow tongue when it is retracted?
On a spike called the hyoid horn
In a sheath under the lower jaw
In the organ of Jacobson
Coiled in the throat pouch
Chameleons retract their hollow tongues onto a spike in the mouth known as the hyoid horn.
Lizards
How do chameleons change the colour of their skin?
With pigment-producing cells called chromatophores
By shedding their skin quickly
By filling their throat pouch with air
By changing their blood flow to the scales
Chameleons change colour through pigment-producing cells called chromatophores.
Lizards
Which is the only chameleon species that occurs in Botswana?
Flap-necked chameleon
Namaqua chameleon
Dwarf chameleon
Jackson's chameleon
Only the flap-necked chameleon occurs in Botswana.
Lizards
How long do flap-necked chameleon eggs take to hatch?
Just over a year
About two weeks
About three months
About three years
The eggs are laid in mid to late summer and take just over a year to hatch.
Amphisbaenia
What does an amphisbaenid do with its tail when threatened?
Waves it in the air to look like the head
Sheds it to distract the predator
Uses it to dig quickly into the soil
Rattles it to make a warning sound
Amphisbaenia means two-headed; when threatened the short tail is waved to resemble the head, so the predator attacks the tail.
Tortoises and terrapins
What is the lower part of a tortoise's shell called?
Plastron
Carapace
Scute
Nuchal
The shell is made up of an upper portion (the carapace) and a base (the plastron).
Tortoises and terrapins
Why are the scutes on a tortoise's shell useful?
Their growth rings can be used to age the animal
Their colour shows the animal's sex
Their number shows how many eggs it has laid
Their shape shows what it eats
Scutes are horny plates of keratin with growth rings like a tree, which makes them useful for ageing the animals.
Tortoises and terrapins
Why do guides never handle tortoises, particularly in the dry season?
Their defensive liquid excretion causes moisture stress
They bite and have a dangerous venom
Their shells break very easily
They carry ticks that spread disease
Tortoises excrete liquid in defence; in dry climates this puts them under major moisture stress, so guides never handle them.
Tortoises and terrapins
How does a terrapin withdraw its head into its shell?
It bends its neck sideways
It pulls its neck straight back
It cannot withdraw its head
It tucks its head under the plastron hinge
Terrapins (sub-order Pleurodira) bend their necks sideways into their shells; tortoises withdraw the neck straight back.
Tortoises and terrapins
According to the manual's table, how do terrapins and tortoises differ in diet?
Terrapins are carnivores; tortoises are herbivores
Terrapins are herbivores; tortoises are carnivores
Both are carnivores
Both are insectivores
The table lists tortoises as terrestrial herbivores and terrapins as fresh-water carnivores.
Tortoises and terrapins
Between which temperatures are chelonians most active?
25 and 30 °C
10 and 15 °C
15 and 20 °C
35 and 40 °C
Chelonians need warmth to become active and are most active between 25 and 30 °C.
Tortoises and terrapins
What is the conservation status of Botswana's tortoises and terrapins?
None of them are threatened
All of them are endangered
They are critically endangered
Only the leopard tortoise is threatened
While some of South Africa's range-restricted tortoises are endangered, none of Botswana's tortoises or terrapins are threatened.
Tortoises and terrapins
Which tortoise is the largest in southern Africa and the only one that can swim?
Leopard tortoise
Serrated tent tortoise
Speke's hinged tortoise
Kalahari tent tortoise
The leopard tortoise is the largest tortoise in southern Africa and the only one that can swim.
Tortoises and terrapins
How is the leopard tortoise told apart from the serrated tent tortoise?
No heavily serrated shell and no nuchal scale
A hinged plastron and a large black head
A much flatter dome to the carapace
A double hook in the upper beak
The leopard tortoise lacks the heavily serrated shell and nuchal scale of the Kalahari or serrated tent tortoise.
Tortoises and terrapins
Which features identify the Okavango hinged terrapin?
A very large black head with yellow patterns
A small brown head with white spots
A heavily serrated shell
A soft, leathery shell
The Okavango hinged terrapin has a hinged plastron and a very large black head with distinctive yellow patterns.
Tortoises and terrapins
How does the Mashona hinged terrapin differ from the Okavango hinged terrapin?
Double hook in the upper beak and usually two chin tentacles
No hinge on the plastron and a lighter shell
A much smaller head and a serrated shell
Three chin tentacles and a smooth beak
The Mashona hinged terrapin is very similar but has a double hook in the upper beak and usually two (not three) tentacles under the chin.
